notes.front: In Scrum, what is a product?
notes.back: A vehicle to deliver value, with a clear boundary, known stakeholders and well-defined users or customers.
notes.explanation: The Scrum Guide defines it inside the Product Goal section, so every Product Goal describes a future state of one such product.
notes.evidence: A product is a vehicle to deliver value. It has a clear boundary, known stakeholders, well-defined users or customers.
notes.example: A hospital’s online appointment system: its boundary is the booking system, the clinic managers are stakeholders and patients are its users.

notes.front: Must a Scrum product be software, or what else can it be?
notes.back: It could be a service, a physical product, or something more abstract.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s definition names services and abstract products, so a product is not limited to software.
notes.evidence: A product could be a service, a physical product, or something more abstract.

notes.front: What is the Product Owner accountable for maximizing?
notes.back: The value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team.
notes.explanation: Value is the first accountability the Guide gives the Product Owner; Product Backlog management is listed after it as an additional one.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team.

notes.front: A director says the Product Owner will be judged on how many items the Scrum Team finishes each Sprint. What is the Product Owner actually accountable for?
notes.back: B) Maximizing the value of the product resulting from the Scrum Team’s work.
notes.explanation: The Guide words the accountability in terms of the product’s value, not the amount of work done.
notes.choices:
A) The number of items the Developers complete each Sprint
B) Maximizing the value of the product resulting from the Scrum Team’s work
C) Keeping the Developers fully busy
notes.choicesExplained: A and C count activity and output; the Guide makes the Product Owner accountable for the value of the product, which finishing more items does not by itself guarantee.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team.

notes.front: Does the Scrum Guide prescribe one way for a Product Owner to maximize value?
notes.back: No. How it is done may vary widely across organizations, Scrum Teams and individuals.
notes.explanation: The Guide states the accountability and leaves the method to each organization, team and person.
notes.evidence: How this is done may vary widely across organizations, Scrum Teams, and individuals.

notes.front: In Product Backlog management, what must the Product Owner do with the Product Goal?
notes.back: Develop it and explicitly communicate it.
notes.explanation: This is the first item in the Guide’s list of what effective Product Backlog management includes.
notes.evidence: Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal

notes.front: In Product Backlog management, what must the Product Owner do about the items that go into the Product Backlog?
notes.back: Create them and communicate them clearly.
notes.explanation: This duty sits second in the Guide’s list of what effective Product Backlog management includes.
notes.evidence: Creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items

notes.front: Which Product Backlog management duty decides the sequence of the items?
notes.back: Ordering the Product Backlog items.
notes.explanation: The Guide says “ordering”, not “prioritizing”; the order is one of the places where the Product Owner’s decisions become visible.
notes.evidence: Ordering Product Backlog items; and,

notes.front: Which Product Backlog management duty is about everyone being able to see and grasp the backlog?
notes.back: Ensuring that the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood.
notes.explanation: It is the last of the four parts of effective Product Backlog management listed under the Product Owner.
notes.evidence: Ensuring that the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood.

notes.front: Which of these is not one of the Product Owner’s Product Backlog management duties?
notes.back: C) Sizing the items.
notes.explanation: Sizing belongs to the Developers who will do the work; the Product Owner’s list covers the goal, the items, their order and transparency.
notes.choices:
A) Ordering the items
B) Explicitly communicating the Product Goal
C) Sizing the items
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are both in the Guide’s list of what effective Product Backlog management includes.
notes.evidence: The Developers who will be doing the work are responsible for the sizing.

notes.front: May the Product Owner hand Product Backlog management work to others?
notes.back: Yes, they may delegate the responsibility, but the Product Owner remains accountable.
notes.explanation: Delegating shares the work; the accountability for the outcome stays with one person.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner may do the above work or may delegate the responsibility to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable.

notes.front: A Product Owner has a business analyst write most of the new backlog items. A sponsor complains that one item is unclear. Who is accountable?
notes.back: A) The Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The Guide lets the Product Owner delegate backlog work but keeps them accountable “regardless”.
notes.choices:
A) The Product Owner
B) The business analyst who wrote the item
C) The Scrum Master
notes.choicesExplained: B did the work but was delegated it, which does not move the accountability. C is accountable for Scrum Team effectiveness, not for the backlog’s content.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner may do the above work or may delegate the responsibility to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable.

notes.front: Can a committee hold the Product Owner accountability?
notes.back: No. The Product Owner is one person, not a committee.
notes.explanation: Being one person does not limit whose needs are covered: the Guide lets that person represent many stakeholders.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog.

notes.front: Whose needs may one Product Owner represent in the Product Backlog?
notes.back: The needs of many stakeholders.
notes.explanation: Those stakeholders are not shut out: the Guide says anyone wanting a change can try to convince the Product Owner.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog.

notes.front: Three department heads propose to share the Product Owner role and vote on the order of the backlog. How does this fit the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: B) It does not: the Product Owner is one person, who may represent all three heads’ needs.
notes.explanation: The Guide rules out a committee but lets one Product Owner represent many stakeholders, who influence the backlog by convincing that person.
notes.choices:
A) It fits, as long as they vote before each Sprint Planning
B) It does not: the Product Owner is one person, who may represent all three heads’ needs
C) It fits if the Scrum Master chairs the vote
notes.choicesExplained: A and C both keep a committee deciding the order, which the Guide excludes whoever chairs it or whenever it meets.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. The Product Owner may represent the needs of many stakeholders in the Product Backlog.

notes.front: For Product Owners to succeed, what must the entire organization do?
notes.back: Respect their decisions.
notes.explanation: The Guide makes this a condition of the Product Owner’s success, not a courtesy, and names where the decisions can be seen.
notes.evidence: For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions.

notes.front: Where are a Product Owner’s decisions visible?
notes.back: In the content and ordering of the Product Backlog, and through the inspectable Increment at the Sprint Review.
notes.explanation: Both places are open to inspection: the backlog’s content and order, and the Increment at the Sprint Review.
notes.evidence: These decisions are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog, and through the inspectable Increment at the Sprint Review.

notes.front: A sales director asks the Developers directly to build a feature that is not in the Product Backlog. Which expectation in the Scrum Guide does this ignore?
notes.back: A) That the entire organization respects the Product Owner’s decisions.
notes.explanation: The Product Owner’s decisions show in the backlog’s content and order; working around them sidesteps what the Guide asks of the whole organization.
notes.choices:
A) That the entire organization respects the Product Owner’s decisions
B) That the Scrum Master approves every new feature
C) That features are only added at the Sprint Retrospective
notes.choicesExplained: B and C describe rules the Guide does not contain: the Scrum Master does not approve features, and the Guide does not restrict backlog changes to the Sprint Retrospective.
notes.evidence: For Product Owners to succeed, the entire organization must respect their decisions. These decisions are visible in the content and ordering of the Product Backlog

notes.front: How can people who want to change the Product Backlog do so?
notes.back: By trying to convince the Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The Guide pairs this with the Product Owner being one person who may represent many stakeholders.
notes.evidence: Those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.

notes.front: A marketing lead has edit rights in the backlog tool and moves her items to the top overnight. What does the Scrum Guide expect her to do instead?
notes.back: C) Try to convince the Product Owner to change the Product Backlog.
notes.explanation: The Guide names convincing the Product Owner as the way to change the backlog; the order reflects the Product Owner’s decisions.
notes.choices:
A) Raise it at the Daily Scrum
B) Ask the Developers to reorder the items for her
C) Try to convince the Product Owner to change the Product Backlog
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Daily Scrum is for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal. B: ordering is part of the Product Owner’s accountability, not the Developers’.
notes.evidence: Those wanting to change the Product Backlog can do so by trying to convince the Product Owner.

notes.front: Who has the authority to cancel a Sprint?
notes.back: Only the Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The Guide gives this authority to nobody else, and links cancellation to the Sprint Goal becoming obsolete.
notes.evidence: Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint.

notes.front: According to the Scrum Guide, when could a Sprint be cancelled?
notes.back: If the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.
notes.explanation: This is the circumstance the Guide gives for cancelling; the decision itself belongs to the Product Owner alone.
notes.evidence: A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.

notes.front: Halfway through a Sprint, the trade fair that the Sprint Goal was built around is called off. The Scrum Master proposes cancelling the Sprint. Who decides?
notes.back: B) The Product Owner, since an obsolete Sprint Goal is a reason to cancel.
notes.explanation: Anyone may raise the idea, but the authority to cancel sits with the Product Owner alone.
notes.choices:
A) The Scrum Master
B) The Product Owner, since an obsolete Sprint Goal is a reason to cancel
C) The Developers, by majority
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the Guide gives the authority to cancel to “only the Product Owner”.
notes.evidence: A Sprint could be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint.

notes.front: Mid-Sprint, the Developers find the work is bigger than expected, but the Sprint Goal is still valid. What does the Scrum Guide describe?
notes.back: A) The Developers negotiate the Sprint Backlog’s scope with the Product Owner, without affecting the Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: The reason the Guide gives for cancelling is an obsolete Sprint Goal; surprises in the work are handled by renegotiating scope.
notes.choices:
A) The Developers negotiate the Sprint Backlog’s scope with the Product Owner, without affecting the Sprint Goal
B) The Product Owner cancels the Sprint
C) The Sprint is extended until the work is done
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Sprint Goal is not obsolete, which is the reason the Guide gives for cancelling. C: a Sprint has a fixed length and is not extended.
notes.evidence: If the work turns out to be different than they expected, they collaborate with the Product Owner to negotiate the scope of the Sprint Backlog within the Sprint without affecting the Sprint Goal.

notes.front: At Sprint Planning, what does the Product Owner make sure of?
notes.back: That attendees are prepared to discuss the most important Product Backlog items and how they map to the Product Goal.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the Sprint Planning plan is created by the collaborative work of the entire Scrum Team.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner ensures that attendees are prepared to discuss the most important Product Backlog items and how they map to the Product Goal.

notes.front: Sprint Planning begins and nobody has seen the items at the top of the backlog or how they relate to the Product Goal. Whose job was it to make sure attendees were prepared?
notes.back: B) The Product Owner’s.
notes.explanation: The Guide puts attendees’ readiness to discuss the most important items, and their link to the Product Goal, on the Product Owner.
notes.choices:
A) The Scrum Master’s
B) The Product Owner’s
C) The stakeholders’
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Scrum Master ensures events take place, but the Guide gives preparing attendees for this discussion to the Product Owner. C: stakeholders may be invited to advise; they are not accountable for preparation.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner ensures that attendees are prepared to discuss the most important Product Backlog items and how they map to the Product Goal.

notes.front: In Sprint Planning’s first topic (“Why is this Sprint valuable?”), what does the Product Owner propose?
notes.back: How the product could increase its value and utility in the current Sprint.
notes.explanation: The proposal is only an input: the whole Scrum Team then shapes the Sprint Goal from it.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value and utility in the current Sprint.

notes.front: After the Product Owner’s proposal at Sprint Planning, who defines the Sprint Goal?
notes.back: The whole Scrum Team, collaborating.
notes.explanation: The Sprint Goal communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders, and it must be finalized before Sprint Planning ends.
notes.evidence: The whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define a Sprint Goal that communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders.

notes.front: A Product Owner arrives at Sprint Planning with a finished Sprint Goal and tells the Developers to adopt it unchanged. What does the Scrum Guide describe instead?
notes.back: C) The Product Owner proposes how the product could gain value; the whole Scrum Team defines the Sprint Goal.
notes.explanation: The Guide splits the work: a proposal from the Product Owner, then a goal the whole team collaborates on.
notes.choices:
A) This is correct: the Sprint Goal is the Product Owner’s alone
B) The Developers define the Sprint Goal without the Product Owner
C) The Product Owner proposes how the product could gain value; the whole Scrum Team defines the Sprint Goal
notes.choicesExplained: A and B each hand the Sprint Goal to one part of the team; the Guide has the whole Scrum Team define it together.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner proposes how the product could increase its value and utility in the current Sprint. The whole Scrum Team then collaborates to define a Sprint Goal

notes.front: When does the Product Owner take part in the Daily Scrum, and in what capacity?
notes.back: When actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, and then as a Developer.
notes.explanation: The Daily Scrum is an event for the Developers of the Scrum Team.
notes.evidence: If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on items in the Sprint Backlog, they participate as Developers.

notes.front: A Product Owner who is not working on any Sprint Backlog items wants to run each Daily Scrum to check progress and hand out tasks. How does this compare with the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: B) The Daily Scrum is for the Developers; the Product Owner participates as a Developer only when working on Sprint Backlog items.
notes.explanation: The Developers are self-managing and plan their own next day; the Guide gives the Product Owner no role in running this event.
notes.choices:
A) It matches the Guide: the Product Owner leads the Daily Scrum
B) The Daily Scrum is for the Developers; the Product Owner participates as a Developer only when working on Sprint Backlog items
C) It matches, provided the Scrum Master agrees
notes.choicesExplained: A and C give the Product Owner a leading role that the Guide does not describe; the event belongs to the Developers.
notes.evidence: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers of the Scrum Team.

notes.front: How does the Scrum Master help the Product Owner with the Product Goal and the Product Backlog?
notes.back: By helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management.
notes.explanation: This is the first of the ways the Guide lists in which the Scrum Master serves the Product Owner.
notes.evidence: Helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management;

notes.front: Serving the Product Owner, what does the Scrum Master help the Scrum Team understand about backlog items?
notes.back: The need for clear and concise Product Backlog items.
notes.explanation: The Guide names the whole Scrum Team here, not only the Product Owner.
notes.evidence: Helping the Scrum Team understand the need for clear and concise Product Backlog items;

notes.front: What kind of product planning does the Scrum Master help establish, as a service to the Product Owner?
notes.back: Empirical product planning for a complex environment.
notes.explanation: Scrum rests on empiricism, and the Guide applies it to product planning as well as to the work of a Sprint.
notes.evidence: Helping establish empirical product planning for a complex environment; and,

notes.front: What does the Scrum Master facilitate, as requested or needed, in serving the Product Owner?
notes.back: Stakeholder collaboration.
notes.explanation: The Guide words this one conditionally: “as requested or needed”.
notes.evidence: Facilitating stakeholder collaboration as requested or needed.

notes.front: A new Product Owner struggles to write a useful Product Goal and asks for help with techniques. Whose service to the Product Owner does the Scrum Guide describe for this?
notes.back: B) The Scrum Master’s.
notes.explanation: Helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition is listed among the ways the Scrum Master serves the Product Owner.
notes.choices:
A) The Developers’
B) The Scrum Master’s
C) The organization’s leadership
notes.choicesExplained: A and C may well help, but the Guide lists this service under the Scrum Master.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Master serves the Product Owner in several ways, including: - Helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management;

notes.front: When several Scrum Teams work on the same product, what should they share?
notes.back: The same Product Goal, Product Backlog and Product Owner.
notes.explanation: The Guide says this when a team grows too large and reorganizes into several cohesive teams focused on one product.
notes.evidence: each focused on the same product. Therefore, they should share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.

notes.front: What should Scrum Teams that become too large consider doing?
notes.back: Reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product.
notes.explanation: The Guide notes smaller teams generally communicate better and are more productive, and puts a typical team at 10 or fewer people.
notes.evidence: If Scrum Teams become too large, they should consider reorganizing into multiple cohesive Scrum Teams, each focused on the same product.

notes.front: A growing product now has three Scrum Teams, and each team has appointed its own Product Owner with its own backlog. What does the Scrum Guide recommend?
notes.back: C) One Product Goal, one Product Backlog and one Product Owner for all three teams.
notes.explanation: The Guide asks teams focused on the same product to share all three, not just one or two of them.
notes.choices:
A) Keep three Product Owners but merge the backlogs
B) Keep three backlogs but set one Product Goal
C) One Product Goal, one Product Backlog and one Product Owner for all three teams
notes.choicesExplained: A and B each keep part of the split; the Guide asks for all three to be shared.
notes.evidence: Therefore, they should share the same Product Goal, Product Backlog, and Product Owner.

notes.front: What can a Product Owner hand to others, and what can they not?
notes.back: The Product Backlog work can be delegated; the accountability cannot, and stays with the Product Owner.
notes.explanation: So a Product Owner who delegates backlog work still answers for it.
notes.evidence: The Product Owner may do the above work or may delegate the responsibility to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable.
